chapters.category: Ethiopic textual tradition • Modern English research translation
chapters.title: Chapter 3 — Adam and Eve in Eden
chapters.sourceNote: Translated afresh into clear modern English from the earliest complete primary-language witness responsibly available for this chapter. No surviving Hebrew Qumran manuscript, Greek excerpt, or early Latin fragment preserves Jubilees 3. The complete wording therefore follows the Ethiopic (Geʽez) text preserved in manuscripts A–D and printed on text pages 9–14 of R. H. Charles’s 1895 critical edition, The Ethiopic Version of the Hebrew Book of Jubilees. No modern English translation was used as the translation base, no commentary was used as Scripture, and no wording absent from the Geʽez witness was supplied.

verses.text: During the six days of the second week, according to God’s word, we brought to Adam all the wild animals, livestock, birds, everything that moves upon the earth, and everything that moves in the water, by kind and form: the wild animals on the first day, livestock on the second, birds on the third, land-moving creatures on the fourth, and water-moving creatures on the fifth.
verses.study: The creatures arrive in an ordered sequence for Adam’s discernment. Human authority begins with attentive recognition of the life God has made.
crossReferences: Genesis 2:19 — God brings the creatures to Adam to see what he will call them
Psalm 8:6–8 — humanity receives responsibility over land, air, and sea creatures

verses.text: Adam gave them all their names. Whatever he called each one became its name.
verses.study: Naming expresses understanding and delegated authority. Adam receives rather than creates the beings whose names he gives.
crossReferences: Genesis 2:19–20 — Adam names every living creature
Genesis 1:5 — naming marks ordered distinction within creation

verses.text: During those five days Adam saw every kind upon the earth, male and female, but he was alone and found no helper corresponding to him.
verses.study: The paired creatures reveal Adam’s solitude. No other earthly kind supplies the mutual human companionship he needs.
crossReferences: Genesis 2:20 — no suitable helper is found for Adam
Ecclesiastes 4:9–10 — companionship provides help that solitude lacks

verses.text: The Lord said to us, ‘It is not good for the man to be alone. Let us make for him a helper corresponding to him.’
verses.study: God himself identifies human isolation as not good. The promised helper corresponds to Adam in shared humanity.
crossReferences: Genesis 2:18 — God declares solitude not good and promises a fitting helper
Genesis 1:26 — divine deliberation precedes humanity’s creation

verses.text: The Lord our God caused a deep sleep to fall upon Adam. While he slept, God took one rib from among his ribs as the beginning of the woman, closed the flesh in its place, and built the woman.
verses.study: The woman is fashioned from Adam’s own embodied life. Her creation displays kinship, divine craftsmanship, and purposeful distinction.
crossReferences: Genesis 2:21–22 — God takes from Adam’s side and builds the woman
Psalm 139:13–14 — human bodies are works of God’s wondrous making

verses.text: God awakened Adam from his sleep. He rose on the sixth day, and God brought her to him. Adam recognized her and said, ‘This one is now bone from my bones and flesh from my flesh. She will be called woman, because she was taken from man.’
verses.study: Adam’s words celebrate recognition rather than possession. Shared bone and flesh affirm the woman’s full correspondence with him.
crossReferences: Genesis 2:22–23 — Adam recognizes the woman as bone and flesh of his own
Ephesians 5:28–30 — marital love is compared with care for one’s own body

verses.text: Therefore man and woman will be one. A man will leave his father and mother, cling to his wife, and they will become one flesh.
verses.study: Marriage forms a new primary bond marked by faithful attachment and bodily unity. Creation becomes the pattern for covenant union.
crossReferences: Genesis 2:24 — leaving, clinging, and one flesh define marriage
Matthew 19:4–6 — Jesus grounds marital permanence in creation

verses.text: Adam was created during the first week, and his wife—his rib—during the second week. She was shown to him afterward. For this reason the command was given concerning impurity: seven days for a male child and twice seven days for a female child.
verses.study: The narrative connects creation’s sequence with Israel’s purification calendar. Embodied birth is placed within ordered holy time.
crossReferences: Leviticus 12:2–5 — childbirth purification begins with seven or fourteen days
Genesis 2:21–23 — the woman’s creation follows Adam’s

verses.text: After Adam completed forty days in the land where he was created, we brought him into the garden of Eden to cultivate and guard it. His wife was brought in on the eightieth day, and after that she entered the garden.
verses.study: Entry into Eden is portrayed as ordered and purposeful. Adam enters to serve and guard, not merely to enjoy.
crossReferences: Genesis 2:15 — Adam is placed in Eden to cultivate and guard it
Numbers 8:15 — ordered preparation precedes entry into holy service

verses.text: For this reason it is written on the heavenly tablets concerning a woman who gives birth: if she bears a male, she remains in her impurity seven days, corresponding to the first week, and remains thirty-three days in the blood of purification. She must not touch anything holy or enter the sanctuary until these days for a male child are complete.
verses.study: The text locates Israel’s purification law in heavenly order. Temporary restriction protects the distinction surrounding sanctuary holiness.
crossReferences: Leviticus 12:2–4 — forty days are completed before contact with holy things
Leviticus 15:31 — Israel is guarded from defiling God’s dwelling

verses.text: If she bears a female, she remains in her impurity for two weeks of days, corresponding to the first two weeks, and sixty-six days in the blood of purification; altogether they are eighty days.
verses.study: The second period completes the chapter’s creation-based correspondence. The law gives defined limits rather than permanent exclusion.
crossReferences: Leviticus 12:5 — purification after a daughter totals eighty days
Leviticus 15:28 — impurity periods end through counted days

verses.text: When she had completed those eighty days, we brought her into the garden of Eden, for it is holier than all the rest of the earth, and every tree planted in it is holy.
verses.study: Eden is treated as sanctuary-like ground. Entry follows completion because its planted life belongs to an especially holy realm.
crossReferences: Ezekiel 28:13–14 — Eden is pictured as God’s holy mountain
Genesis 2:8–9 — God himself plants Eden’s trees

verses.text: Therefore the statute concerning a woman who bears a male or female was established: she must touch no holy thing and enter no sanctuary until the days appointed for a son or daughter are complete.
verses.study: The stated principle brings both cases under one concern: reverence for holy things and places during a temporary bodily condition.
crossReferences: Leviticus 12:4–6 — purification is completed before sanctuary approach
Hebrews 9:8–10 — bodily regulations govern access under the first covenant

verses.text: This is the law and testimony written for Israel so that they may observe it through all their days.
verses.study: The creation narrative again becomes written instruction. Israel is called to sustained remembrance rather than occasional interest.
crossReferences: Deuteronomy 6:1–2 — statutes are observed throughout Israel’s days
Psalm 78:5–7 — testimony is established for later generations

verses.text: In the first week of the first jubilee, Adam and his wife lived in the garden of Eden for seven years, cultivating and guarding it. We gave him work and taught him to do everything suitable for cultivation.
verses.study: Edenic life includes meaningful labor and instruction. Work belongs to the garden’s goodness before sin distorts it.
crossReferences: Genesis 2:15 — cultivation and guardianship are Adam’s first vocation
Proverbs 12:11 — faithful cultivation yields provision

verses.text: He cultivated the garden. He was naked without knowing it and was not ashamed. He guarded the garden from birds, wild animals, and livestock, gathered its fruit and ate, and set aside what remained for himself and his wife, including what was to be preserved.
verses.study: Unashamed openness coexists with responsible provision. Adam protects, gathers, eats, and preserves within the garden’s ordered abundance.
crossReferences: Genesis 2:25 — the man and woman are naked without shame
Genesis 2:16 — the garden’s trees are freely given for food

verses.text: After the full seven years he completed there, in the second month of the eighth year, on the seventeenth day, the serpent came near the woman and said, ‘Did God command you not to eat from every tree of the garden?’
verses.study: The serpent opens by distorting the breadth of God’s generosity. A single boundary is recast as universal deprivation.
crossReferences: Genesis 3:1 — the serpent questions God’s command
2 Corinthians 11:3 — the serpent’s cunning seeks to corrupt faithful devotion

verses.text: She said, ‘God told us, “Eat from all the fruit of the garden’s trees, but do not eat fruit from the tree in the middle of the garden, and do not touch it, lest you die.”’
verses.study: The woman recalls both permission and prohibition. Life in abundance still includes trust expressed through a commanded limit.
crossReferences: Genesis 2:16–17 — broad permission is joined to one prohibition
Deuteronomy 30:19–20 — life is found in loving and obeying God

verses.text: The serpent said, ‘You certainly will not die. God knows that on the day you eat from it your eyes will open; you will become like gods and know good and evil.’
verses.study: Temptation directly contradicts judgment and recasts mistrust as enlightenment. The creature invites humanity to define wisdom apart from God.
crossReferences: Genesis 3:4–5 — the serpent denies death and promises opened eyes
John 8:44 — the devil’s speech is characterized by falsehood

verses.text: The woman saw that the tree was desirable and pleasing to the eyes and that its fruit was good for food. She took some and ate.
verses.study: Sight, desire, and appetite converge in disobedient action. Created goodness is seized outside the Creator’s command.
crossReferences: Genesis 3:6 — the woman sees, desires, takes, and eats
1 John 2:16 — bodily desire, visual desire, and pride oppose the Father’s will

verses.text: After first covering her shame with fig leaves, she gave some to Adam, and he ate. His eyes opened, and he saw that he was naked.
verses.study: The promised opening brings shame rather than glory. Sin spreads through shared participation and alters self-perception.
crossReferences: Genesis 3:6–7 — both eat and recognize their nakedness
Romans 5:12 — sin and death enter human experience through transgression

verses.text: He took fig leaves, sewed them together, made a covering for himself, and covered his shame.
verses.study: Humanity’s first response is self-made concealment. The covering treats exposure but cannot undo disobedience.
crossReferences: Genesis 3:7 — fig leaves are sewn into coverings
Psalm 32:3–5 — concealed sin requires confession, not merely hiding

verses.text: God cursed the serpent and remained angry with it forever.
verses.study: The deceiver is placed under divine judgment. Evil speech does not escape the Creator’s lasting verdict.
crossReferences: Genesis 3:14–15 — God curses the serpent and announces conflict
Revelation 20:2, 10 — the ancient serpent reaches final judgment

verses.text: He was angry with the woman because she listened to the serpent and ate. He said, ‘I will greatly multiply your pain and sorrow. In pain you will bear children; your turning will be toward your husband, and he will rule over you.’
verses.study: The judgment reaches childbirth and marital life. Relationships intended for joy now bear pain and domination.
crossReferences: Genesis 3:16 — pain in childbirth and marital rule follow the transgression
1 Timothy 2:14 — the woman’s deception is recalled in apostolic instruction

verses.text: To Adam he said, ‘Because you listened to your wife’s voice and ate from the tree that I commanded you not to eat from, the ground is cursed because of you. It will produce thorns and thistles for you. You will eat bread by the sweat of your face until you return to the earth from which you were taken, for you are earth and to earth you will return.’
verses.study: Adam’s judgment falls upon work, ground, and mortality. His vocation continues, but now through resistance, pain, and eventual return to dust.
crossReferences: Genesis 3:17–19 — cursed ground, toil, thorns, and return to dust follow Adam’s sin
Romans 8:20–22 — creation is subjected to frustration and groans

verses.text: God made garments of skin for them, clothed them, and sent them out from the garden of Eden.
verses.study: God provides a more durable covering even as he expels them. Judgment and care appear together.
crossReferences: Genesis 3:21–24 — God clothes the pair before banishing them
Psalm 104:1–2 — God’s own glory is pictured through clothing and covering

verses.text: On the day Adam left the garden, at sunrise in the morning, he offered a pleasing fragrance: frankincense, galbanum, stacte, and aromatic spices, from the day he covered his shame.
verses.study: Adam answers exile with fragrant worship. The first movement outside Eden is directed toward the God whose presence he has lost.
crossReferences: Exodus 30:34–36 — stacte, galbanum, and frankincense form holy incense
Psalm 141:2 — prayer is likened to incense before God

verses.text: On that day the mouths of all wild animals, livestock, birds, walkers, and moving creatures were closed so they could no longer speak, for before then they had all spoken with one another in one language and one tongue.
verses.study: The fall fractures communication across creaturely life. A formerly shared speech gives way to silence and separation.
crossReferences: Genesis 3:1–5 — the serpent speaks with the woman before judgment
Romans 8:19–22 — the nonhuman creation shares the consequences of human fallenness

verses.text: God sent every fleshly creature out of the garden of Eden. Every creature was scattered by kind and form to the places made for them.
verses.study: Expulsion affects the whole garden community. Creatures return to appointed habitats as Eden’s protected fellowship closes.
crossReferences: Genesis 3:23–24 — humanity is sent out and access to Eden is guarded
Psalm 104:10–18 — creatures inhabit the places God appoints

verses.text: Among all wild animals and livestock, Adam alone was given a covering for his shame.
verses.study: Clothing marks humanity’s distinct moral awareness after sin. Bodily covering answers shame unique to the human transgressors.
crossReferences: Genesis 3:21 — God clothes Adam and his wife
1 Corinthians 12:23 — bodily parts associated with shame receive greater covering

verses.text: For this reason it is prescribed on the heavenly tablets concerning all who know the judgment of the law: they must cover their shame and not expose themselves as the nations expose themselves.
verses.study: The narrative becomes an ethic of modesty. Knowledge of divine judgment shapes how the body is publicly honored.
crossReferences: Leviticus 18:6–19 — Israel is forbidden to uncover nakedness unlawfully
Exodus 20:26 — worship must not expose nakedness

verses.text: At the new moon of the fourth month, Adam and his wife left the garden of Eden and lived in the land of Elda, the land where they had been created.
verses.study: The calendar records exile precisely. Humanity returns to ordinary created ground outside the sanctuary-like garden.
crossReferences: Genesis 3:23 — Adam is sent to work the ground from which he was taken
Genesis 2:8 — the garden is planted after the man’s formation

verses.text: Adam named his wife Eve.
verses.study: The naming anticipates life and future generations beyond judgment. Hope remains in the woman’s identity.
crossReferences: Genesis 3:20 — Adam names his wife Eve because she is mother of all living
Genesis 4:1 — Eve later bears the first son

verses.text: They had no child until the first jubilee was completed. Afterward Adam knew her.
verses.study: Human generation begins outside Eden in appointed time. Marital union carries life forward in a fallen world.
crossReferences: Genesis 4:1 — Adam knows Eve and she conceives
Ecclesiastes 3:1–2 — birth belongs to appointed time

verses.text: He cultivated the land as he had been taught in the garden of Eden.
verses.study: Adam’s vocation survives expulsion. Knowledge learned in Eden equips faithful labor amid cursed ground.
crossReferences: Genesis 3:23 — Adam is sent out to cultivate the ground
Genesis 4:2 — cultivation and shepherding continue in the next generation

explanation.heading: Chapter teaching and context
paragraphs: Chapter 3 moves from ordered creation into human companionship. Adam names the creatures but finds no corresponding helper, so God builds the woman from his side. Their shared bone and flesh grounds marriage as a union of faithful attachment and one flesh.

The chapter connects creation’s sequence with Israel’s childbirth purification laws and portrays Eden as especially holy ground. Its aim is text-grounded: bodily life, sacred time, and sanctuary access are ordered before God, while temporary impurity has defined limits.

Adam and Eve’s garden service is good, but the serpent distorts God’s generosity and denies judgment. Desire becomes disobedience; opened eyes bring shame; work, birth, relationships, creatures, and mortality all bear the result. Yet God clothes the pair, Adam worships, and life continues outside Eden.

The ending preserves both loss and vocation. Eden closes, creatures scatter, modest covering becomes a moral duty, and Adam returns to ordinary land. Still he cultivates as he was taught, Eve bears a life-giving name, and human history proceeds under judgment with traces of divine care.

crossReferences: Genesis 2:18–25 — the woman is formed and marriage becomes one flesh
Genesis 3:1–24 — temptation, transgression, judgment, clothing, and exile from Eden
Leviticus 12:1–8 — childbirth purification governs approach to holy things
Exodus 30:34–38 — fragrant spices are appointed for sacred incense
Psalm 8:4–8 — humanity receives authority over other creatures
Ezekiel 28:12–17 — Eden and God’s holy mountain are linked
Matthew 19:4–6 — creation grounds the permanence of marriage
Romans 5:12–19 — Adam’s transgression brings sin and death
Romans 8:18–23 — creation shares corruption while awaiting renewal
Revelation 22:1–5 — access to the tree of life returns in the healed city
